en: Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Grove.

Now, the great brahmin Vāsiṣṭha, an old friend of the Blessed One, while walking and wandering for his daytime diversion, approached the place where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he exchanged various greetings with the Blessed One—conducive to friendship and joy—and sat down to one side. Perceiving that the brahmin Vāsiṣṭha was seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Vāsiṣṭha, why are you so emaciated, discolored, with long hair, beard, nails, and body-hair, and with such a parched voice?"
Vāsiṣṭha said: "O Gautama, because of my month-long fasts, I am thus emaciated, discolored, with long beard, hair, nails, and body-hair, and my voice is weak when I speak.

Then the Blessed One, although he already knew, questioned the brahmin Vāsiṣṭha: "Vāsiṣṭha, do you observe the fast endowed with the eight noble factors? Do you keep watch during the fortnight of miracles? Vāsiṣṭha said: "What, O Gautama, does one become who observes the fast endowed with the eight noble factors and keeps watch during the fortnight of miracles?"

The Blessed One said: "O Vāsiṣṭha, he enjoys both divine and human pleasures. Vāsiṣṭha said: "If, Gautama, these Śākyas were to observe the fast endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones and attend to it during the fortnight of miracles, they too would enjoy both divine and human pleasures."

The Blessed One said: "Vāsiṣṭha, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that these Śāla trees would understand the meaning of what has been spoken; such a thing cannot occur. However, young man, having concluded that it is impossible, I shall speak based on a conceptual analogy. If these Śāla trees were to understand the meaning of what I have spoken, they too would enjoy both divine and human sensual pleasures. Vāsiṣṭha asked: "How, O Gautama, does one who has observed the fast endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones enjoy divine and human sensual pleasures?"

The Blessed One said: "In this case, Vāsiṣṭha, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family, desiring to observe the fast endowed with the eight noble limbs, should rise early in the morning and approach a learned brahmin or some other wise person. Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placing his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, he speaks thus:"

Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, abstained from taking life—having laid aside the rod and laid aside the weapon, being modest and compassionate toward all beings, including even the smallest creatures such as ants and termites—even so do I, [name], from this moment until the coming night and until the rising of the sun tomorrow, in the interval between these times, abandon the taking of life and abstain from taking life.
By this first factor, I train in accordance with, conform to, and emulate the training of those noble Arhats.

Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, dancing, singing, music, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, ornaments, and cosmetics, high beds and large beds, and eating at improper times—having desisted from eating at improper times—even so I, named so-and-so, from this moment until the coming night and until the rising of the sun tomorrow, in the interval between these times, [shall abandon] taking what is not given.

Having abandoned unchastity, false speech, the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, dancing, singing, music, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, ornaments, and cosmetics, high and large beds, and eating at improper times—I abstain from eating at improper times. By this eighth limb, I train in accordance with, follow, and imitate the training of those noble Arhats.
Thus a second and a third time.

Young man, this is called the fast endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones. When one has thus observed the fast endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones, it becomes of great fruit and great benefit; it leads to the attainment of the deathless, culminates in the deathless, and conduces to the realization of the fruit of the deathless. Having thus observed the fast of the eight limbs of the noble ones, one enjoys both divine and human pleasures.

In this way, Vasiṣṭha, it is impossible to grasp the measure of the merit of a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who observes the fast endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones; nor can one grasp the extent of that fruit of merit or the ripening of the fruit of merit. Rather, because of the abundance of merit, it is reckoned as a "great mass of merit."

Vasiṣṭha, it is just as if these five great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarayū, Sindhu, and Vakṣu—were to flow together and converge at a single point. In that case, it would be impossible to grasp the measure of the water, saying, "There is this much water," or "a jar of water," or "a hundred jars of water," or "a hundred thousand jars of water. Rather, because of the vastness of the water, it comes to be designated simply as a "great mass of water."
What do you think, Vāsiṣṭha? Would anyone be able to grasp the measure of the water of the great ocean, or [say] "there is this much water"?
